concepts.name: How EF Core translates parameterized collections (Contains over a list)
Type predicates: if-and-only-if semantics, inference and assertion functions
React 19 form Actions with useActionState and useFormStatus

questions.prompt: In EF Core 10 on SQL Server, `context.Blogs.Where(b => ids.Contains(b.Id))` runs with an `ids` array of 8 values. What SQL does EF send by default?

choices.text: `IN (1, 2, ...)`: the values are inlined, so every list gets its own plan
`OPENJSON(@ids)`: a single JSON parameter, the same SQL for any list size
`IN (@ids1, ..., @ids10)`: one parameter per value, padded to fewer shapes
One query per value, combined with `UNION ALL` so each part can use an index seek

questions.explanation: EF 10's default sends each value as its own scalar parameter and pads the list (8 values become 10 parameters), so the planner knows roughly how many values there are while only a few SQL shapes reach the plan cache. Inlined constants (EF 7 and earlier) bloated the plan cache; the single `OPENJSON` parameter of EF 8 hid the cardinality from the planner. You can choose another mode with `UseParameterizedCollectionMode` or per query with `EF.Constant`.

sources.title: What's New in EF Core 10
sources.claim: Up to EF 7 parameterized collections were inlined as constants (plan cache bloat); EF 8 sent one JSON array parameter unpacked with OPENJSON (planner loses the cardinality); EF 10 by default sends one scalar parameter per value, padded (8 values become 10 parameters); UseParameterizedCollectionMode(ParameterTranslationMode.Constant) or EF.Constant(ids) choose another mode.

questions.prompt: With TypeScript 5.5 or later, `scores` is `(number | undefined)[]`. What is the type of `scores.filter(s => !!s)`?

choices.text: `number[]`, because TypeScript infers `s is number` from the truthy check
`(number | undefined)[]`: `false` could also mean `s` was `0`
`number[]`, but only when `strictNullChecks` is off in the project config
`never[]`, because `!!s` returns a boolean, not the original element type

questions.explanation: TypeScript 5.5 infers type predicates for callbacks like `s => s !== undefined`, giving `number[]`. A predicate `s is number` means "if and only if": a `false` result must mean `s` isn't a number. `!!s` is also false for `0`, so no predicate is inferred, and the type stays `(number | undefined)[]`. That protects a real bug: the filter silently drops zero scores.

sources.title: TypeScript 5.5
sources.claim: TypeScript 5.5 infers a type predicate such as `x is Bird` for `filter(bird => bird !== undefined)`, but not for `filter(score => !!score)`, because type predicates mean 'if and only if' and a false result could also mean the score was 0.

questions.prompt: You are moving a React 19 "Add to cart" form from `onSubmit` with `useState` flags to Actions. Explain how `useActionState` and `useFormStatus` fit together, and one mistake that leaves the submit button never showing a pending state.

model_answer.summary: `useActionState` turns an action into form state plus a dispatch function you pass to `<form action>`, and `useFormStatus` lets a component inside that form read its pending status; calling `useFormStatus` in the component that renders the `<form>` itself never reports pending.
key_points: `useActionState(action, initialState)` returns `[state, dispatchAction, isPending]`; pass `dispatchAction` to `<form action={...}>`, and the action receives the previous state and the `FormData` and returns the next state, such as an error message
Submissions through a form action run in a Transition, and several dispatches are queued and run one after another, each receiving the previous result
`useFormStatus` returns `pending`, `data`, `method` and `action` for its parent `<form>` only, so call it in a child such as a `SubmitButton` rendered inside the form
Calling `useFormStatus` in the same component that renders the `<form>` is the mistake: it doesn't track that form, so `pending` is never true

questions.explanation: Actions replace hand-written loading and error flags: React tracks the pending state and the result for you. `useFormStatus` reads context from the nearest parent form, which is why it must live below the `<form>` in the tree; `isPending` from `useActionState` is the alternative in the form component itself.

sources.title: useActionState
sources.claim: useActionState(action, initialState) returns [state, dispatchAction, isPending]; passed to <form action>, React wraps the submission in a Transition and calls the action with the previous state and the FormData, queuing several dispatches sequentially.

sources.title: useFormStatus
sources.claim: useFormStatus returns pending, data, method and action for a parent <form> only; called in the same component that renders the <form>, `pending` is never true, so call it from a component rendered inside the form.

questions.prompt: After upgrading from EF Core 8 to EF Core 10, a query using `ids.Contains(x.Id)` sends different SQL. Explain the ways EF has translated parameterized collections, the trade-off of each, and how you choose one.

model_answer.summary: EF has inlined the values as constants, sent one JSON array parameter, and (EF 10's default) sent one padded parameter per value; each trades plan-cache reuse against giving the planner the list's cardinality, and you can pick the mode globally or per query.
key_points: Inlining the values as constants (EF 7 and earlier) produces different SQL for each list, causing plan cache misses and bloat

One JSON array parameter unpacked with `OPENJSON` (EF 8) keeps one SQL text and plan for every list, but hides the list's cardinality from the planner, so the plan may suit only small or only large lists
EF 10 sends one scalar parameter per value and pads the count (8 values become 10 parameters), keeping few SQL shapes while giving the planner the cardinality
Choose with `UseParameterizedCollectionMode(ParameterTranslationMode....)` in the provider options, or per query with `EF.Constant(ids)` and similar, because the best mode depends on your data

questions.explanation: No single translation is right for every query: plan reuse and accurate cardinality pull in opposite directions. EF 10's padded parameters are a compromise, and the configurable mode lets you override it where measurements show another choice is faster.

sources.title: What's New in EF Core 10
sources.claim: Up to EF 7 parameterized collections were inlined as constants (plan cache bloat); EF 8 sent one JSON array parameter unpacked with OPENJSON (planner loses the cardinality); EF 10 by default sends one scalar parameter per value, padded (8 values become 10 parameters); UseParameterizedCollectionMode(ParameterTranslationMode.Constant) or EF.Constant(ids) choose another mode.

questions.prompt: `isOrder(x: unknown): x is Order` and `assertIsOrder(x: unknown): asserts x is Order` both check a parsed API response `data`. How do they narrow `data` differently?

choices.text: Both narrow for the rest of the scope; only `assertIsOrder` checks at run time
`isOrder` narrows inside the `if` that uses it; `assertIsOrder` narrows after
`isOrder` narrows after the call; `assertIsOrder` narrows in a `try` block only
Neither narrows unless `Order` is a class, since both rely on `instanceof`

questions.explanation: A type predicate returns a boolean, so `if (isOrder(data))` narrows `data` to `Order` in that branch (and to the rest of the union in `else`). An assertion function returns nothing and throws when the check fails, so after `assertIsOrder(data);` the value is narrowed for the rest of the scope. Both work with any type; the check inside is ordinary code you write.

sources.title: Narrowing
sources.claim: A function returning `pet is Fish` is a type predicate: when it is called in an `if`, TypeScript narrows the variable to `Fish` in that branch and to the rest of the union in the `else` branch.

sources.title: TypeScript 3.7
sources.claim: An assertion function (`asserts val is string`) throws when the check fails and narrows the value for the rest of the containing scope, while a type predicate (`val is string`) returns a boolean and narrows only within the `if` that uses it.

choices.text: `pending` turns true only when the `action` prop is a URL, not a function
`useFormStatus` works only together with `useActionState`, not on its own
`placeOrder` must call `startTransition`, or the form is never pending
`useFormStatus` reads a parent `<form>`, not one this component renders

questions.explanation: `useFormStatus` reports on the `<form>` above the calling component, not one it renders itself, so here `pending` is always false. Move the button into a `SubmitButton` component rendered inside the form and call `useFormStatus` there. A function `action` is exactly what it tracks, and form actions already run in a Transition.

sources.title: useFormStatus
sources.claim: useFormStatus returns pending, data, method and action for a parent <form> only; called in the same component that renders the <form>, `pending` is never true, so call it from a component rendered inside the form.

questions.prompt: You are moving a React 19 "Add to cart" form from `onSubmit` with `useState` flags to Actions, with `useActionState` and `useFormStatus`. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: `useActionState` returns `[state, dispatchAction, isPending]`
The action receives the previous state and the form's `FormData`
`useFormStatus` must be called in a component rendered inside the `<form>`
Calling `useFormStatus` in the component that renders the `<form>` tracks that form
Several quick submits run their actions in parallel, each with the initial state

questions.explanation: `useActionState(action, initialState)` returns the state, a dispatch function you pass to `<form action>`, and `isPending`; with a form, the action receives the previous state and the `FormData` and returns the next state. Several dispatches are queued and run one after another, each receiving the previous result. `useFormStatus` reports only on a parent `<form>`, so call it in a child such as a `SubmitButton`: called in the component that renders the form itself, `pending` is always false.

sources.title: useActionState
sources.claim: useActionState returns [state, dispatchAction, isPending]; the action receives the previous state and, with a form, the FormData; React queues multiple dispatchAction calls and runs them sequentially, each receiving the previous result.

sources.title: useFormStatus
sources.claim: useFormStatus returns status only for a parent form and must be called from a component rendered inside it; it won't track a form rendered in the same component, where pending is always false.

questions.prompt: After upgrading from EF Core 8 to EF Core 10, a query using `ids.Contains(x.Id)` sends different SQL. Which statements about translating parameterized collections are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Inlining the values as constants makes new SQL per list, bloating the plan cache
EF 8's single JSON array parameter hides the list's cardinality from the planner
EF 10 sends one parameter per value and pads the count, such as 8 values to 10
EF 10's default gives every list one SQL text and one cached plan, whatever its size
The mode is fixed per provider, with no way to choose it for a single query

questions.explanation: Inlined constants (EF 7 and earlier) produce different SQL for each list, causing plan cache misses and bloat. EF 8's single JSON array parameter keeps one SQL text and plan but deprives the planner of the list's length, so the plan may suit only small or only large lists. EF 10 sends one scalar parameter per value, padding the count (8 values become 10 parameters) so there are few SQL shapes while the planner still sees the cardinality. You choose the mode globally with `UseParameterizedCollectionMode` or per query with `EF.Constant` and similar.

sources.title: What's New in EF Core 10
sources.claim: Inlined constants caused plan cache misses and bloat; EF 8's JSON array parameter keeps one plan but hides cardinality from the planner; EF 10 by default translates each value into its own parameter and pads the list (8 values become 10 parameters); the mode can be set with UseParameterizedCollectionMode or per query with EF.Constant.
